title: Aprapransa with Palm Cream
author: Fran Osseo-Asare
desc: Skim off the palm oil rising to the top — you should end up with a cup and a half to two cups — then stir corn flour in until it pulls away from the sides.
longDesc: The better-sourced aprapransa, with full quantities and two real cues. Two thirds of a cup of adzuki beans, salted cod, six shallots, ten ounces of smoked whiting, half a habanero, about three quarters of a large tin of cream of palm fruit, ten small tomatoes, powdered shrimp and two cups of toasted corn flour. The first cue is the skim: take off the palm oil rising to the top, and you should end up with about a cup and a half to two cups of oil. The second is the finish: stir the corn flour in constantly to prevent lumps until the mass pulls away from the sides.
ingredients: 6 shallots, or 1 1/4 cups chopped onion (300 ml)
1 large tin cream of palm fruit — you will use about 3/4 of it
2 cups toasted corn flour, tom brown (500 ml)
About 10 small tomatoes, or several large
2 tbsp powdered shrimp or crayfish (30 ml)
steps: Cook the adzuki beans until tender.
Build the palm fruit soup with the shallots, tomatoes, habanero, smoked whiting, salted cod and powdered shrimp.
Simmer until the palm oil rises to the top.
Skim off the palm oil rising to the top — you should end up with about 1 1/2 to 2 cups of oil.
Set most of the soup aside, keeping some in the pot.
Slowly stir the corn flour into the remaining soup, stirring constantly to prevent lumps.
Stir in the rest of the soup.
Keep stirring and cooking until it pulls away from the sides.
Serve with the skimmed palm oil spooned over.
chefTips: The skim is the step most versions omit and it is the one that makes the dish. A cup and a half to two cups of oil comes off, and it goes back on at the end rather than staying in the mass.
Pulls away from the sides is the finishing cue, the same test as banku and akple. That is when the corn flour has cooked.
Add the corn flour to only PART of the soup first, then stir the rest in. Two stages, and it is how you avoid lumps in two cups of flour.
Adzuki beans are her substitute for Ghanaian small red beans, declared as such. Any small red bean works.
Toasted corn flour, not cornmeal. This is the same tom brown that binds ayikple and dzowoe.
Smoked whiting and salted cod together — two preserved fish doing different jobs, the whiting for body and the cod for salt and depth.
King crab legs are offered as a substitution for the crab of the classic version. The dish is traditionally made with crab.
commonMistakes: Leaving the palm oil in rather than skimming it.
Adding all the corn flour to all the soup at once.
Stopping before it pulls away from the sides.
Leaving out the salted cod, which carries the savour.
sources: Adapted from 'Aprapransa: delicious Ghanaian onepot meal', betumiblog.blogspot.com, 26 March 2013. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'Fran'. Yield as printed: 'Serves 6'. Quantities agreed across a first and third fetch; the second returned a summary.

Ingredients exactly as printed: 2/3 cup adzuki beans (150 ml); about 1 tablespoon (15 ml) of salted cod; 6 shallots (or substitute 1 1/4 cups of chopped onion) (300 ml); about 10 oz of smoked whiting (300 g); about 1/2 Habanero pepper; a large can of cream of palm fruit (you'll use about 3/4 of it); 2 cups of Tom Brown flour (toasted corn flour) (500 ml); ~10 small tomatoes or several large tomatoes; 2 tablespoons (30 ml) powdered shrimp/crayfish.

THE TWO CUES, both verbatim and both better than anything in the other documented aprapransa: 'scoop off the palm oil rising to the top—you should end up with about 1 1/2 to 2 cups of oil'; and 'slowly stir in the corn flour to the remaining soup, stirring constantly to prevent lumps. Stir in the rest of the soup and keep stirring and cooking until it pulls away from the sides.'
DECLARED SUBSTITUTIONS: adzuki beans for Ghanaian small red beans; and king crab legs where crab is wanted.

WHY THIS IS PUBLISHED ALONGSIDE GHA010 RATHER THAN REPLACING IT: the other entry comes from an UNBYLINED page and is the only source giving the soup-to-cornmeal ratio in ladles and tablespoons, plus the palm-taste cue — 'taste to see if the fresh taste of the palm is completely gone'. This version has a named author, full quantities, and the skim and pull-away cues. The two are complementary and both are kept, with the sourcing of each stated.

THE NAMES, quoted: 'Along with its Twi name aprapransa, it's also called akpledzi (Ga or Ewe), apragyaa (Fante), or bɔbɔe (Ewe), or akplijii.' And: 'I first met it in the Eastern Region'. She adds that THE EWE ATTRIBUTION IS NOT EXCLUSIVE.

THE COMMUNITY QUESTION REMAINS UNSETTLED, as at GHA010: a Ghana Broadcasting Corporation piece says the dish 'originates with the GaDangme people'; this author first met it in the Eastern Region under its Twi name; and a Ghana News Agency piece presents 'Apregyae' as Fante festival food. Three named sources, three attributions. The community field records the dispute.

The same authors' cookbook entry, 'Toasted Cornmeal One-Pot with Crab' in The Ghana Cookbook, 6 servings, Medium, carries the SAME naming headnote. Its quantities are not visible behind the publisher's paywall.

ON CREAM OF PALM FRUIT: the tinned palm pulp, the same product used in the palm nut soup at GHA019. Three quarters of a large tin is the printed amount, which is unusually precise for a tinned ingredient.
storage: 3 days refrigerated. It sets very firm.
reheating: Low heat with water or the reserved palm oil to loosen.
healthBenefits: Adzuki beans supply plant protein, folate and soluble fibre.
Palm fruit cream is very high in provitamin-A carotenoids and tocotrienols.
Smoked fish and dried shrimp add protein, calcium and iodine.
Skimming the oil removes a substantial share of the fat from the mass itself.
culturalNote: Aprapransa is a one-pot that collapses soup and swallow into a single mass, and the skimmed palm oil spooned back over the top is what makes it look like a celebration dish rather than a porridge. Its four names across four peoples is the clearest sign of how far a good coastal dish travels.
